title: Israel Election Puts Netanyahu's Coalition on the Line After Three Years of War
dek: Israelis vote Tuesday in the first national election since the October 7 attacks. Pre-election polls pointed to a fractured Knesset, making coalition negotiations as important as the vote itself.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: A ballot paper used in an Israel Bar Association election, illustrating the voting process

keyPoints: Israel's October 27 vote is its first national election since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks and ensuing war.
Al Jazeera reported that pre-election polls showed neither the pro-Netanyahu nor opposition blocs on course for the 61 seats needed to form a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
The result may lead to extended coalition bargaining; polls are not election results and seat projections can shift with turnout and parties crossing the electoral threshold.
body:
Israel goes to the polls Tuesday in a parliamentary election that will test Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's grip on power and the country's political direction after a prolonged conflict and domestic division. It is the first national vote since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks. The outcome could affect security policy, accountability debates and the balance between the governing coalition and its opponents.

## A close contest without a clear majority

The Knesset has 120 seats, and a coalition needs 61 to govern. Al Jazeera's October 26 review of polls published before the survey blackout said neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition appeared positioned to reach that threshold. One poll by public broadcaster KAN projected 52 seats for the opposition alliance and 50 for Netanyahu's bloc, leaving the remainder with smaller and unaffiliated parties. Those are projections, not final tallies.

The fragmented field means the first count may not settle who governs. Parties will need to negotiate with potential coalition partners, and the electoral threshold can determine which lists enter parliament and how seats are distributed. If no viable majority emerges, negotiations could be prolonged or another political impasse could follow.

## Issues beyond the premiership

The campaign has centered on the aftermath of the October 7 security failures, the wars and their human and economic costs, military-service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox communities, judicial reform and national security. The election will not itself resolve those issues, but it will select the lawmakers who decide the next government's composition and agenda.

For international observers, the near-term watch is therefore two-stage: turnout and seat allocation on Tuesday, followed by coalition talks. Any market or diplomatic response will depend not just on which party finishes first but on what governing arrangement can command a majority and what policy it can sustain.

## How the parliamentary arithmetic works

Israel's parliament has 120 seats, and parties must clear a 3.25% vote threshold to win representation. That rule means a party's national vote share alone does not translate directly into seats: lists that fall short do not enter parliament, and their voters do not produce seats for those parties. The result can change the balance between blocs, particularly when polling suggests neither side is close to a majority.

Al Jazeera reported that polls published before the campaign's survey blackout projected 52 seats for the opposition alliance and 50 for Netanyahu's bloc in one KAN survey, with the remainder going to unaffiliated or smaller parties. Those figures describe one poll, not a consensus or the final distribution. Differences in turnout, late decisions, and whether smaller parties cross the threshold can all alter the calculation.

This uncertainty helps explain why the identity of the largest party may not immediately determine who becomes prime minister. After votes are counted, leaders have to assemble a coalition that can command confidence in the Knesset. Negotiations may involve compromises over security policy, judicial changes, religious exemptions and the handling of inquiries into the October 7 failures. The ability to put together a workable majority, not just a narrow election-night lead, is the central institutional test.

The immediate reporting discipline matters too: polls are snapshots taken before voting, and seat projections are estimates based on modeled support. They should not be written as a prediction of a specific government. The reliable facts entering Tuesday are the date of the election, the 120-seat chamber, the 61-seat majority threshold and the absence of a clear majority in the latest polls described by the sources.
